screens__DarkPool__DarkPoolPositionScree.s6: Data comes from the 13F reports the fund files with the SEC at the end of each quarter: how many shares it holds and their value. The reports don't list trades — a “trade” here is the change in share count between two reports, at the quarter-end price. The average price uses quarter-end prices at each change. Today's value and return use the stock's live price and the share count in the latest report.

screens__Learning__LearningScreen.s2:
Who is this course for?
Traders who want to go deeper into day trading and learn to spot large flows and liquidity in the market.

What will you learn?
Tools for analyzing market structure and liquidity — including Smart Money Concepts (Order Blocks, FVG, Premium & Discount and more) — and how to apply them to day trading stocks and options.

You'll also learn to build a daily trading plan, manage trades in real time, and combine flow analysis with disciplined risk management.

screens__DarkPool__utils__stockActEstima.s2:
Members of Congress report trades under the STOCK Act. Each filing has a wide dollar range (e.g. $1,001–$15,000) and a trade date — not an exact amount or share count.

We show the range as reported. Current holdings come from Quiver by BioGuide ID, when available. We don't invent share counts or reconstruct portfolios from the reported ranges.

«Since the trade» is the ticker's price change from the open on the trade day vs. the live quote (or Quiver's PriceChange when available) — not the position's profit or loss.

screens__DarkPool__utils__trumpHoldings.s2: Trades from Quiver and Unusual Whales (deduplicated). Most filings give an amount range (e.g. $1,001–$15,000) rather than an exact amount. For each trade, a share count is derived from the range and the price on the trade day, and the value uses today's market price; sales reduce the oldest position first. So a range is shown: from the lower bound of all filings to the upper bound. The chart and weights use the middle of the range. This is an estimate from the filings — not Trump's full net worth.

screens__DarkPool__utils__tradeDetailHon.s1: About the numbers on this screen
screens__DarkPool__utils__tradeDetailHon.s3:
The quantity and price per share come from the Form 4 filing. The value is their product — not a separate quote.

The price at the top is a live quote. «Since the trade» compares it to the price in the filing.

We don't have a 10b5-1 flag or the security type. Code P/S is a purchase/sale per the SEC — not proof of an open-market vs. private transaction.

utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s1: The Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee sets the US benchmark rate. Rate hikes aim to curb inflation but slow growth, while cuts stimulate growth. FOMC decisions are the most market-moving economic event.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s2: The base rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. It's the key rate the Fed sets, and it affects every rate in the economy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s3: Total assets held by the Federal Reserve. Expanding the balance sheet injects money into the economy and supports stocks, while shrinking it drains liquidity and pressures markets.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s4: A qualitative economic report the Fed publishes 8 times a year, based on interviews with executives and business people. It comes out two weeks before the FOMC meeting and hints at the expected rate decision.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s5: Detailed minutes of the FOMC meeting, covering the discussions and considerations behind the rate decision. Published 3 weeks after the meeting, revealing the committee members' views.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s6: The Fed Chair's press conference after a rate decision. The market parses every word to understand the Fed's intentions for future rates.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s7: The yield on the 10-year US Treasury. It's the risk-free rate used as the basis for pricing all assets, including mortgages and stocks. A rising yield reflects inflation concerns or risk.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s8: The yield on the 2-year Treasury. It's the most sensitive to Fed rate decisions and reflects the market's rate expectations for the next two years.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s9: The yield on the 30-year Treasury. Reflects long-term expectations for inflation and economic growth.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s10: The yield on the 3-month Treasury bill. Used as a base for measuring the yield curve and reflects the shortest-term rate in the economy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s11: The spread between the 10-year and 2-year Treasury yields. An inverted curve, when the 2-year yields more than the 10-year, is considered a warning of an approaching recession.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s12: Total credit banks extend to businesses and consumers. A rise reflects banks' willingness to lend and a strong economy; a decline signals weakness or tighter credit conditions.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s13: The Consumer Price Index measures the change in prices of a fixed basket of goods and services. A rising CPI reflects high inflation and may lead the Fed to raise rates. The Fed's inflation target is 2% per year.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s14: CPI excluding food and energy. Food and energy prices are very volatile, so Core CPI is considered a cleaner measure of the underlying inflation trend. The Fed focuses on it more than headline CPI.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s15: The Producer Price Index measures price changes at the wholesale and production level. A rising PPI signals higher production costs that are likely to pass to consumers, so it's a leading indicator for CPI.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s16: PPI excluding food and energy. Shows the underlying production cost trend beyond commodity price swings.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s17: Personal Consumption Expenditures is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. It's broader than CPI and adjusts dynamically to changes in spending habits. The Fed's official target: 2% per year.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s18: PCE excluding food and energy. The Fed Chair watches it daily, and it's the Federal Reserve's official inflation target.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s19: The Import Price Index measures the change in prices of goods imported into the US. A rise reflects external inflationary pressure or a weaker dollar.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s20: The Export Price Index measures the change in prices of goods exported from the US. A rise reflects strong demand or a stronger dollar.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s21: The energy component of CPI, including oil, gas and electricity. Very volatile due to its dependence on global energy prices.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s22: The food component of CPI. Volatile due to weather, seasonality and agricultural commodity prices.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s23: Nonfarm payrolls measure the number of jobs added or lost in the economy last month. It's the key gauge of labor market health and one of the most market-moving events. Released on the first Friday of every month.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s24: The unemployment rate is the share of the labor force looking for work and not employed. Low unemployment reflects a strong economy, but too low can drive wage growth and inflation.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s25: Weekly jobless claims are the most frequent gauge of labor market health. Below 200,000 reflects a strong labor market; above 300,000 signals weakness.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s26: ADP's private employment report measures jobs added in the private sector. Released two days before the official NFP and used as an early forecast.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s27: Job openings measure demand for workers. A high number reflects a strong labor market but can lead to wage growth and inflation.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s28: Average hourly earnings measure the pace of wage growth. Fast growth signals inflationary pressure through rising labor costs.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s29: The labor force participation rate measures the share of the working-age population that is employed or looking for work. A decline may signal people giving up on job searches.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s30: Gross domestic product is the value of all goods and services produced in the country in a quarter. It's the broadest measure of the economy's size and health. Growth of 2-3% is considered healthy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s31: Inflation-adjusted GDP, showing real economic growth. It's the most accurate measure of economic development.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s32: The quarterly or annual growth rate of GDP. Above 4% is considered strong growth, below 1% a slowdown, and negative a recession.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s33: Retail sales measure store sales volume. Since 70% of the US economy is consumption, this reflects consumer health and the direction of the economy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s34: Retail sales excluding autos. Gives a steadier picture of the consumption trend since auto sales are very volatile.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s35: Output at factories, mines and utilities. A rise reflects high demand and a strong economy. It's considered a leading indicator — rising before growth and falling before a recession.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s36: Output in the manufacturing sector. A significant part of industrial activity and a sign of the sector's health.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s37: The share of production capacity actually in use. Above 80% reflects a hot economy and busy factories; above 82% raises inflation concerns due to capacity shortages.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s38: Business inventory levels. Rising inventories signal weak demand, while falling inventories reflect strong demand. Inventory levels affect future production decisions.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s39: Orders for durable goods such as machinery, vehicles and appliances. Rising orders signal business confidence and investment, and are a leading indicator of future production.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s40: Total new orders to factories. An order today means production tomorrow, so it's a leading indicator for industrial activity and employment.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s41: Personal consumption expenditures make up about 70% of US GDP. A rise signals a strong consumer and a growing economy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s42: A survey of purchasing managers in manufacturing. Above 50 reflects expansion, below 50 contraction. It's a leading indicator that predicts economic trends before they happen.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s43: A survey of purchasing managers in the services sector. Since services are about 80% of the US economy, it matters more than ISM Manufacturing.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s44: S&P Global's manufacturing activity index. Similar to ISM but with a different methodology and a broader sample.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s45: S&P Global's services activity index. Reflects the services sector, the backbone of the economy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s46: A combination of the manufacturing and services PMIs. Gives an overall picture of private sector activity.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s47: The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index measures consumer optimism about the economy. Optimistic consumers tend to buy and spend more, which drives growth.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s48: The University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey. It also includes consumers' inflation expectations, which can become reality if the public expects high inflation.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s49: The business confidence index measures executives' confidence in the economy. High confidence leads to investment and expansion; low confidence leads to cutbacks.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s50: The number of new construction projects started. Real estate is about 15% of the economy and drives employment and sales of building materials and furniture. A rise reflects strong housing demand.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s51: The number of building permits approved. A leading indicator for Housing Starts — a permit today means construction in 3-6 months.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s52: Existing home sales reflect housing demand and real estate market health. They make up most real estate activity.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s53: New home sales signal future demand and the state of construction. Less volatile than Existing Home Sales.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s54: The National Association of Home Builders sentiment index. Above 50 reflects good building conditions, below 50 poor conditions.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s55: The broadest US home price index. Measures price changes in the 20 largest cities and reflects the real estate market trend.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s56: The difference between exports and imports. A trade deficit means imports exceed exports, which weakens the dollar over time.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s57: The value of goods and services exported from the US. A rise strengthens the dollar and signals strong global demand for American products.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s58: The value of goods and services imported into the US. A rise reflects strong domestic demand but weakens the dollar.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s59: The balance of all economic transactions with the world, including trade, investment and transfers. A large deficit signals reliance on foreign funding.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s60: The S&P 500 volatility index, known as the "fear index". A VIX below 15 reflects a calm market; above 25 reflects fear and panic. As a rule, VIX rises when stocks fall.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s61: The index of the 500 largest US companies. Considered the main US market index and the benchmark for the overall market.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s62: The index of 30 leading industrial companies. The oldest and best-known index, but less representative than the S&P 500.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s63: The technology companies index. Reflects the performance of the tech and growth sector.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s64: The DXY index measures the dollar's value against 6 major currencies. A strong dollar hurts US exports but makes imports cheaper and lowers inflation.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s65: The dollar-euro exchange rate. The most traded pair in the world, reflecting the relationship between the two largest economies.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s66: The dollar-Japanese yen exchange rate. Very sensitive to rate policy and considered a gauge of global risk.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s67: The dollar-British pound exchange rate. Reflects the relationship between the US and UK economies.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s68: The oil price directly affects energy costs and is a key component of inflation. A higher oil price raises CPI and pressures the Fed to raise rates.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s69: West Texas Intermediate is the US benchmark for crude oil prices. It's the basis for oil pricing in North America.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s70: Brent is the global benchmark for oil prices. It's the basis for pricing about two thirds of the world's oil.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s71: The European Central Bank sets interest rate policy for the eurozone. Higher rates in Europe strengthen the euro and weaken the dollar.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s72: The Bank of England sets the UK's base rate. Its policy affects the pound and global investors.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s73: The Bank of Japan runs a unique monetary policy with negative rates. Policy changes can affect global currency markets.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s74: The total income of all Americans. Higher income gives purchasing power and drives consumption and growth.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s75: Consumer spending is the main engine of the US economy. A rise signals consumer confidence and a strong economy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s76: A weekly economic index that combines multiple data points into an up-to-date picture of the economy.
utils__economicIndicatorExplanations.s77: An economic indicator reflecting one aspect of the economy's health. Stronger-than-expected data usually supports the dollar and pressures stocks on rate-hike fears. Weaker-than-expected data may support stocks but weaken the dollar.

services__courseService.s3:
Who is this course for?
Traders and investors who already know the market basics and want to master options trading and advanced strategies.

What will you learn?
How to find high-quality options swing trades, perform advanced technical analysis, spot high-probability entry and exit zones, understand how options actually behave, manage risk properly and build a consistent long-term trading strategy.

The goal is to give you a clear, structured method so you can make data-driven decisions instead of acting on emotion or guesswork.
services__courseService.s6: From 0 to an independent stock market trader
services__courseService.s7:
Who is this course for?
Beginners and traders who want to learn from the basics up to advanced technical analysis, swing trading and day trading stocks.

What will you learn?
Tools for analyzing market structure and liquidity — including Smart Money Concepts (Order Blocks, FVG, Premium & Discount and more) — and how to apply them to day trading stocks and options.

You'll also learn to build a daily trading plan, manage trades in real time, and combine flow analysis with disciplined risk management.

services__courseService.s69:
Who is this course for?
Anyone who wants to start trading or investing in the stock market, even with no prior experience or knowledge.

What will you learn?
The Trading Foundations course was built to give you a strong professional foundation in the stock market. You'll learn how the market works, the different asset types, how to open a trading account, how to read charts, how to spot trends, the principles of technical analysis, how to manage risk properly and how to build a structured trading plan.

By the end you'll have a broad understanding of trading and all the tools you need to move confidently to the next stage.
